small_guidance:
- Add BLOCK_M to the autotune sweep (try 64/128/256) instead of fixing it at 128 — with M=128 the grid is only 1 row-tile so larger BLOCK_M=128 with bigger BLOCK_N (e.g. 256) will increase per-program work; also try BLOCK_M=64 with BLOCK_N=256 to expose more parallelism across the 4090's 128 SMs.
- Cast loaded `a` and `b` tiles to `tl.float16` (or use `tl.dot(..., out_dtype=tl.float32, input_precision='tf32')`) to ensure tensor-core path is used; current `allow_tf32=True` is correct but verify with explicit `input_precision='tf32'` and try `num_stages=4-5` with BLOCK_K=64 to better overlap the K=16384 loop.
- Add a K-tail mask only if needed (K=16384 is divisible by 32/64/128 so unmasked loads are fine) — but add `even_k`-style configs with BLOCK_K=256 and num_warps=8 since K is very large and fewer iterations may help.
large_guidance:
- Problem is M=128, N=16384, K=16384 — a "skinny-tall" GEMM with only 128 rows. Consider a split-K (or stream-K) strategy: partition the K dimension across multiple programs per output tile and atomic-add (or two-stage reduce) to fully utilize all 128 SMs, since the current grid is only (1 row-tile) × (N/BLOCK_N) = 64-128 programs which barely saturates the GPU.
- Alternatively, persistent kernel with one program per N-tile that streams all M rows in registers (M=128 fits easily in a single BLOCK_M tile), eliminating the row-tile dimension entirely and letting each program own its full N column slice with maximum K-loop pipelining.
- Use fp16/bf16 inputs internally (cast x and weight_t at load time) to double tensor-core throughput on the 4090; the min/sub epilogue in fp32 is unaffected. Memory bandwidth on the 16384×16384 weight (1 GB in fp32, 512 MB in fp16) is the dominant cost.
